No slides were given for this lecture. The notes of Alessa, Alsalamah and Alomar word for word, in their own order (green), every gift (red) under the part it belongs to.

Notes

Breast Examination

Inspection

Inspect both breasts for skin edema/peau d'orange, nipple position (normal vs retracted), and visible masses/skin abnormalities.

  • Most common presentation of breast cancer in Saudi Arabia → painless breast mass. 436
  • Retroareolar ER/PR+ HER2− mass with nipple retraction, node-negative (recall without choices) → central lumpectomy removing the nipple–areola complex + SLNB + radiotherapy (or mastectomy + SLNB), then endocrine therapy. 441
Notes

Palpation

Use the palmar surface of fingers/hand. Systematically examine the entire breast using either 4 quadrants (upper outer, upper inner, lower outer, lower inner) or the clock-face method. Start with superficial palpation (mainly tenderness); if a non-tender/deeper mass is felt → deep palpation.

ANY BREAST MASS — DESCRIBE
Side + exact location/quadrant/clock position, approximate size, mobility, fixation to skin or underlying tissues, tenderness. Complete one breast, then examine the contralateral breast.
Notes

Axillary Examination

Examine both axillae for lymphadenopathy — right axilla with the left hand, left axilla with the right hand. Support the patient's arm so axillary muscles stay relaxed. Describe nodes: number, size, discrete vs matted, mobility/fixation.

Notes

Examination for Metastatic Disease

Breast cancer commonly metastasizes to viscera and bone. Examine the abdomen for ascites, organomegaly/visceral metastases, and the back/skeleton for evidence of bone metastases.
  • Breast cancer 5 years ago, now 3 weeks of neck pain without trauma → spinal MRI (bone metastasis/cord compression). 439
Notes

Investigations

Breast assessment relies heavily on radiology + biopsy; blood tests are relatively less important initially. Main imaging: breast ultrasound, mammography, breast MRI.
  • 70-year-old man with an ulcerating breast mass and axillary nodes → initial step mammogram (then biopsy) — not excision or antibiotics. 438 ×5
Notes

BI-RADS

BI-RADS = standardized breast imaging reporting/classification system used for mammography, ultrasound, and MRI.

CategoryMeaningAction
0Incomplete assessmentAdditional imaging/modality required
1Normal/negativeRoutine follow-up
2Benign findingRoutine follow-up
3Probably benign; malignancy risk <2%Short-interval/close follow-up (e.g. 3–6 months)
4Suspicious abnormalityBiopsy
5Highly suspicious for malignancyBiopsy
6Biopsy-proven malignancy—
EXAM-IMPORTANT
BI-RADS 4 or 5 → tissue biopsy required.
Notes

Breast Biopsy

Core Needle Biopsy

Lesion TypeApproach
PalpableClinical core biopsy under local anesthesia
Non- palpable/deepImage-guided: (1) ultrasound-guided if visible on US, (2) stereotactic mammography-guided if mammographically visible, (3) MRI-guided if not adequately visualized otherwise (technically most difficult)
These procedures can generally be performed under local anesthesia.
  • Palpable 3-cm mass after history & exam → imaging, then biopsy 437 ×3; mammogram is ordered to look for microcalcifications 438; young woman with bloody discharge → ultrasound. 438
Notes

Why Not Immediately Perform Excisional Biopsy?

AVOID EXCISING AN UNDIAGNOSED MASS
If malignancy is unexpectedly found: appropriate oncologic margins may not have been taken, margins may be positive, and definitive surgery may need to be repeated. Therefore → core biopsy first or refer appropriately rather than removing an unknown mass.
  • Best initial diagnostic step for a breast mass → core biopsy (not FNA or surgery). 434 ×2
Notes

Information From Core Biopsy

InformationDetails
1. DiagnosisMalignant vs benign
2. Histological typeDuctal carcinoma (most common), lobular carcinoma (second most common); less common: mucinous, papillary, medullary
3. Tumor gradePathological differentiation — Grade 1 (well differentiated), Grade 2 (intermediate), Grade 3 (poorly/undifferentiated)
4. Hormone receptorsER, PR — determine benefit from hormonal/endocrine therapy
5. HER2HER2-positive tumors (~15%) are biologically aggressive; determines eligibility for HER2-targeted biological therapy
6. Ki-67Proliferation marker — low (e.g. 5%) = slow-growing; very high (e.g. 90%) = rapidly proliferating/aggressive with greater metastatic potential
GRADE ≠ STAGE
Grade = pathology (differentiation); stage = extent of disease clinically/anatomically. Do not confuse the two.
Notes

Biological Subtypes of Breast Cancer

Based mainly on ER, PR, HER2, Ki-67, and grade. Two relatively aggressive groups: triple-negative and HER2-positive. Luminal cancers are generally less aggressive.

SubtypeER/PRHER2Grade / Ki-67Behavior
Luminal AER+, PR+NegativeGrade 1; Ki-67 low (~≤10%)Very favorable prognosis — best profile
Luminal BER+, usually PR+May be negativeGrade 2–3; Ki-67 higher (~40–50%)More aggressive than Luminal A; may have positive nodes
HER2- positiveVariablePositive—Aggressive; HER2-targeted therapy available
Triple- negativeER−, PR−Negative—Very aggressive, especially in younger patients; no hormonal/HER2 target — chemotherapy is the major systemic treatment
  • 95-year-old, devastating comorbidities, ulcerating T3N0M0 luminal A (ER/PR ~100%, Ki-67 5%, grade 1) → hormonal therapy only. 439 ×3
  • Triple-negative with one positive axillary node → neoadjuvant chemotherapy, then surgery. 442 ×4
Notes

TNM / Clinical Staging

After completing imaging, biopsy, and metastatic evaluation → classify as stage I–IV.

StageDescription
I–IIEarly breast cancer — relatively small/localized tumor, may have limited regional lymph-node involvement
IIILocally advanced — advanced local/regional disease, remains confined to breast/regional nodal territory
IVMetastatic — disease detected outside the breast and regional nodal areas; poor prognosis, 5-year survival <18%; treatment overwhelmingly non- surgical/systemic (~95%): chemotherapy, hormonal therapy, biological/targeted therapy
  • Single most important prognostic factor → number of involved axillary nodes. 429 ×3
  • Locally advanced (stage III, skin involvement, 3 nodes) invasive ductal carcinoma → neoadjuvant chemotherapy first. 436 ×3
Notes

Metastatic Screen

VERY IMPORTANT OSCE STEP
Once biopsy confirms breast cancer, do not immediately jump to surgery or chemotherapy before assessing for metastases. Metastatic screen: CT chest, CT abdomen, CT pelvis, bone scan. Purpose → determine whether disease is stage IV.
TYPICAL CLINICAL SEQUENCE
History → examination → mammogram/US → biopsy → confirmed cancer → metastatic screen → staging → management.

Exam-important: students commonly forget the metastatic screen after receiving a positive breast biopsy result.

Metastatic screen after a positive biopsy — CT chest, abdomen, pelvis + bone scan — before surgery or chemo. Commonly forgotten OSCE step. Sequence: history → exam → mammogram/US → biopsy → metastatic screen → staging → management.
  • Metastatic (brain + bone) triple-negative cancer → keyed palliative care (the doctor: stage IV is treated systemically — palliative chemotherapy; no breast surgery). 436
Notes

Inflammatory Breast Cancer

RARE BUT EXTREMELY AGGRESSIVE
Described as even more aggressive clinically than typical TNBC.
Notes

Presentation

May closely mimic a breast abscess: redness, hotness, swelling, possible fluctuation, fever/inflammatory features — this can lead to misdiagnosis as infection.

WHY ANTIBIOTICS MAY SEEM TO HELP
Malignancy can produce a surrounding inflammatory reaction. Antibiotics/treatment may temporarily improve some inflammatory features → false reassurance while underlying cancer persists.
  • "Cellulitis" recurring 5 times despite antibiotics → skin biopsy. 441
Notes

Avoiding Missed Diagnosis

If treating presumed breast abscess: follow the patient closely, approximately every 2 weeks, ensuring the lesion is progressively resolving. A

persistent/non-resolving or enlarging lesion → reconsider diagnosis and biopsy (the solid component if concern is high).

KEY PRINCIPLE
Inflammatory breast cancer does not resolve as a simple abscess would. A persistent/enlarging inflammatory breast lesion requires tissue diagnosis. Exam-important: the key to avoiding missed diagnosis is follow-up + biopsy of a non-resolving lesion.
Notes

Breast Cancer Treatment

Treatment divides into: (1) systemic therapy (treats the whole body) and (2) locoregional therapy (treats the breast and axilla).

Notes

Systemic Therapy

Three major modalities: hormonal/endocrine therapy (oral), chemotherapy (IV), biological/targeted therapy (usually IV). Most patients require at least one systemic modality depending on tumor biology.

Notes

Hormonal Therapy

Indication: ER-positive breast cancer (no meaningful benefit if ER-negative). Duration usually 5–10 years.

Notes

HER2-Targeted Biological Therapy

Indication: HER2-positive breast cancer — given IV at intervals, commonly every ~3 weeks.

Notes

Chemotherapy

Strong indications: triple-negative breast cancer, HER2-positive breast cancer, and many Luminal B tumors depending on risk/biology. Typical schedule: every ~3 weeks, 4, 6, or 8 cycles (usually not >8).

Notes

Systemic Treatment by Biological Subtype

SubtypeTypical Systemic Treatment
Luminal AMainly hormonal therapy alone
Luminal BOften chemotherapy + hormonal therapy
HER2-positiveChemotherapy + HER2-targeted biological therapy; add endocrine therapy if hormone-receptor positive
Triple negativeChemotherapy — no benefit from endocrine or HER2-targeted therapy
  • ER−, PR−, HER2+ → trastuzumab (Herceptin) (tamoxifen, letrozole and goserelin need ER+). 442
Notes

Locoregional Therapy

Targets: breast, axilla. Breast surgery options: (1) mastectomy, (2) breast-conserving surgery / wide local excision / lumpectomy.

Notes

Lumpectomy / Breast-Conserving Surgery

DEFINITION
Lumpectomy = removal of the malignant tumor with a surrounding safety margin (~1–1.5 cm) — malignant lesions require an oncological margin; benign lesions do not. General goal: preserve the breast whenever oncologically safe.
RADIOTHERAPY REQUIREMENT
Breast-conserving surgery = lumpectomy + radiotherapy. Lumpectomy must generally be followed by radiotherapy to "sterilize" the remaining breast. If radiotherapy cannot be given → breast-conserving surgery is generally unsuitable → mastectomy.
  • DCIS (calcifications) → lumpectomy + radiotherapy. 441
Notes

Mastectomy

Mastectomy = removal of the whole breast. Types: simple, skin-sparing, nipple-sparing (detailed differences not emphasized).

  • ER+ cancer in a 65-year-old with previous bilateral breast radiation for Hodgkin's → simple mastectomy (can't re-irradiate). 442
  • Paget disease of the nipple = a superficial manifestation of an underlying breast cancer (eczema-like nipple change → biopsy). 426
Notes

When Mastectomy May Be Required / Lumpectomy Unsuitable

ReasonExplanation
1. Multicentric diseaseCancer in separate areas/quadrants → difficult/impossible to remove adequately while conserving the breast
2. Multifocal diseaseMultiple tumor foci may prevent adequate conservation depending on extent
3. Extensive DCISLarge area of ductal carcinoma in situ may require mastectomy
4. Large tumor, small breastRemoving a large lesion may leave an insufficient breast; neoadjuvant chemotherapy may shrink a chemo-sensitive tumor enough for later lumpectomy
5. BRCA1/BRCA2 positivityRelative (not absolute) contraindication — mastectomy may be preferred given hereditary risk
6. PregnancyRadiotherapy cannot be given during pregnancy; if diagnosed late, surgery may proceed followed by delivery and later RT
7. Previous breast/chest radiationRepeat radiation may be unsafe — increases tissue toxicity and risk of secondary malignancy such as sarcoma
8. Collagen vascular/skin diseaseE.g. lupus — may flare/worsen with radiotherapy
OTHER PRACTICAL BARRIERS TO RADIOTHERAPY
Cost, long distance from a radiotherapy center, inability to remain in the treatment city for ~1–1.5 months, social/logistical limitations. Even if lumpectomy + RT is technically possible, an informed patient may choose mastectomy.

Lecture summary: aim for lumpectomy + radiotherapy when safely possible; if lumpectomy or the required RT is contraindicated/unfeasible → mastectomy.

Notes

Ductal Carcinoma In Situ — DCIS

DEFINITION
DCIS = non-invasive precursor/early form of ductal breast carcinoma. Breast malignancy may be heterogeneous/"mosaic" — DCIS in one area and invasive cancer in another. Often non-palpable, frequently detected on mammography as suspicious microcalcifications. Major aim of screening mammography = detect disease at this pre-invasive/very early stage.

Suspicious microcalcifications → biopsy. If DCIS: treatment is primarily surgical — local excision if suitable, mastectomy if extensive. Prognosis is generally excellent when appropriately treated.

  • Most common type of breast cancer → invasive ductal carcinoma ("intraductal" in the recall). 437
Notes

Axillary Surgery

In most operable breast cancer patients, breast surgery is accompanied by assessment/surgery of the axillary lymph nodes (exceptions in selected groups such as some elderly/very low-risk patients). Two approaches: axillary lymph node dissection (ALND), sentinel lymph node biopsy (SLNB).

  • Purpose of sentinel node biopsy → assess the extent of lymphatic involvement (staging the axilla). 441
Notes

Axillary Lymph Node Dissection

DEFINITION & MORBIDITY
ALND = removal of multiple/all relevant axillary lymph nodes — the axilla may contain approximately 20–30 lymph nodes. Traditional operation used for decades; still required with gross/obvious malignant axillary nodal disease. Major morbidity: lymphedema (up to ~40%), shoulder dysfunction, other axillary morbidity. Despite morbidity, grossly malignant axillary disease must be adequately treated — cancer control takes priority.
Notes

Sentinel Lymph Node Biopsy

Preferred in a clinically non-grossly involved axilla to reduce morbidity. Sentinel node = first draining lymph node(s) receiving lymph from the breast — usually ~3 important nodes sampled rather than removing 20–30.
  • Breast mass with clinically and radiologically benign-looking nodes → breast-conserving surgery + sentinel node biopsy. 439 ×3
Notes

Principle

Organs drain through lymphatic channels to regional lymph nodes: lower limb/genital region/buttock → inguinal nodes; upper limb/breast/upper back → axillary nodes. Cancer cells, bacteria, or foreign material entering breast lymphatics travel toward the first draining axillary node.

Notes

Technique

Inject breast/periareolar region with radioactive tracer and blue dye

1 2 3 4

Tracer/dye travels through lymphatics to the sentinel node

Axillary incision; identify the blue node and/or radioactive node using a gamma probe Remove sentinel node(s) and send to pathology

The fact that a node is blue/hot does not mean it is malignant — it only identifies it as the sentinel draining node.
Notes

Frozen Section

Rapid intraoperative pathological assessment may be performed. If malignant nodal disease is found → may proceed to further axillary treatment/dissection. If negative → extensive ALND may be avoided.

Notes

Benefit

ProcedureLymphedema Risk
ALND~40%
SLNB~3–4%
PRACTICAL RULE
Choose sentinel lymph node biopsy unless the axilla is grossly involved with malignant nodes.
Choose SLNB unless the axilla is grossly involved.
Notes

Lymphedema

Results from loss/disruption of axillary lymphatic drainage after extensive nodal surgery — produces chronic swelling of the ipsilateral upper limb. Many treatments exist, but established lymphedema can be difficult to treat effectively. This morbidity is a major reason SLNB replaced routine ALND for clinically node-negative disease.

Notes

Interval Breast Cancer

DEFINITION
Breast cancer diagnosed between two scheduled screening mammograms despite a previous apparently normal mammogram — may have been too subtle/small to detect previously and becomes more obvious before the next scheduled screen. Approximately 10–15% of breast cancers may present this way. Does not automatically mean someone made an error — some cancers were genuinely radiologically occult at the earlier study.
Notes

Genetic / BRCA Testing

Not every breast cancer patient automatically requires genetic testing.

INDICATIONS
Diagnosis at <50 years
Triple-negative breast cancer
Male breast cancer
Family pattern involving breast + ovarian cancer
Other features suggesting hereditary breast cancer

Important hereditary genes: BRCA1, BRCA2. Genetic testing and surgical implications should be discussed with the patient as part of multidisciplinary/shared decision-making.

  • BRCA1 is associated with breast (and ovarian) cancer. 437 ×4
Notes

Breast Cancer Screening

MAIN GOAL
Detect cancer before it becomes clinically palpable, particularly DCIS/suspicious malignant microcalcifications.
Notes

Screening Age

Determined by each country's national screening program. Average-risk screening commonly begins around 40–50 years (routine screening generally does not begin before 40 in average-risk women). Higher-risk women may start earlier, e.g. around 30 years. Screening may continue into older age, approximately up to 75 years, depending on program/patient factors.

Notes

Breast MRI — Indications

No single universal indication for every breast cancer patient. May be useful in:

Young patients
Patients with breast implants
Before and after neoadjuvant chemotherapy (assess tumor response)
BRCA/genetically high-risk patients
Cases where mammography/ultrasound are insufficient or less sensitive
Notes

Complications of Breast/Axillary Surgery

General: bleeding/hematoma, infection/wound complications.

BREAST/AXILLARY-SPECIFIC
Seroma, shoulder dysfunction/reduced movement, sensory disturbance/numbness related to axillary surgery, lymphedema.
Notes

Chemotherapy Response

Tumor sensitivity to chemotherapy is assessed after initiating treatment — there is no simple preliminary "test dose" analogous to testing for an antibiotic reaction. After starting chemotherapy, monitor clinical/imaging response to determine whether the tumor is shrinking/responding.

Notes

Mastery Checklist

BI-RADS 4 or 5 always requires tissue biopsy; BI-RADS 3 gets short-interval follow-up (malignancy risk <2%), not biopsy 1
Never proceed to excisional biopsy for an undiagnosed mass — core biopsy first, to avoid inadequate margins if malignant 2
3 Grade is pathological differentiation; stage is anatomical extent of disease — never conflate the two
4 Biological subtype is defined by ER/PR/HER2/Ki-67/grade: Luminal A (best prognosis) → Luminal B → HER2-positive and triple-negative (most aggressive)
Triple-negative = ER−/PR−/HER2− → chemotherapy is the only systemic option, since there's no hormonal or HER2 target 5
After a confirmed biopsy, always perform a metastatic screen (CT chest/abdomen/pelvis + bone scan) before jumping to treatment — this is a commonly 6
missed OSCE step
Inflammatory breast cancer can mimic an abscess and may transiently improve with antibiotics — a non-resolving or enlarging "abscess" needs biopsy of the solid component
Breast-conserving surgery = lumpectomy + radiotherapy — if RT can't be given, mastectomy is the fallback, not lumpectomy alone
Multicentric/multifocal disease, extensive DCIS, large tumor relative to breast size, BRCA positivity, pregnancy, prior chest radiation, and collagen vascular disease are the classic reasons lumpectomy may be unsuitable
10 DCIS is non-invasive, often non-palpable, and typically detected as microcalcifications — prognosis is excellent with appropriate surgical treatment
11 Choose sentinel lymph node biopsy over ALND unless the axilla is grossly involved — SLNB cuts lymphedema risk from ~40% to ~3–4%
12 A blue/hot sentinel node just marks the first draining node — it does not by itself mean the node is malignant
Interval cancers (~10–15%) diagnosed between screening rounds don't automatically indicate a missed diagnosis — some lesions are genuinely occult at 13
the earlier study
14 Genetic/BRCA testing is targeted, not universal — consider it for age <50, triple-negative, male breast cancer, or a breast+ovarian family pattern
